title: Where Does North Korea’s Nuclear Program Stand in 2026?
gist: An IAEA report of August 28 documents a second uranium enrichment facility under construction at Yongbyon, able to house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, alongside an expanded, operating annex at Kangson; with inspectors expelled for nearly two decades, satellite imagery shows North Korea's nuclear program expanding on multiple fronts.

insights.claim: The IAEA reported to its Board of Governors on August 28, 2026 that North Korea is building a second uranium enrichment facility at its Yongbyon nuclear complex.
insights.speaker: Piergiorgio Pescali
insights.so_what: Expanded fissile-material production raises the ceiling on North Korea's arsenal size and hardens Korean-peninsula risk premia.

insights.claim: The new Yongbyon enrichment building could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, and operates alongside an already-running expanded annex at the Kangson enrichment site.
insights.speaker: Piergiorgio Pescali
insights.so_what: Multiple parallel enrichment sites imply a step-up in weapons-grade uranium output; watch for regional defense spending responses in South Korea and Japan.
insights.quote: The new facility could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades

insights.claim: North Korea's nuclear program in late 2026 is visibly expanding on multiple fronts at once.
insights.speaker: Piergiorgio Pescali
insights.so_what: A multi-front expansion argues against expectations of a freeze or denuclearization deal.
insights.quote: a program that is visibly expanding, on multiple fronts at once
insights.locator: Nearly two decades after international inspectors

insights.claim: Nearly two decades after international inspectors were expelled, satellite imagery and open-source analysis are the only windows into Pyongyang's nuclear program.
insights.speaker: Piergiorgio Pescali
insights.so_what: Intelligence on North Korea relies on commercial satellite and OSINT providers, supporting demand for those capabilities.
insights.locator: Nearly two decades after international inspectors

insights.claim: The IAEA identified the new facility by matching satellite images of its construction with state-media photos of Kim Jong Un's June 2026 visit, in which centrifuges and cascades resembling those at known enrichment sites were visible.
insights.speaker: Piergiorgio Pescali
insights.so_what: Pyongyang's own propaganda is disclosing capability, suggesting it wants its enrichment expansion to be seen as leverage.
insights.locator: The agency identified the new two-story building
